title: The Spandakarika
author: vasugupta
attributionNote: Ascribed to Vasugupta, who is said in the tradition to have found the Shiva Sutras on the rock at Mahādeva near Srinagar; the verses of the Spanda tradition were arranged and commented on by his followers, and Kṣemarāja wrote the longer commentary the library holds beside other works of the school. GRETIL's e-text carries the verses alone, in the file's own numbering.
description: The Spandakārikā is the poem of the school of recognition: that the universe is the vibration of a single consciousness, that this vibration is present in every act of perception and in every breath, and that the yogi who recognises it in the moment of a desire, a fear or a wonder sees the whole world as Shiva's own play. Its fifty-three verses, in four sections of the outpouring, the arising, the descent into the individual and the recognition of one's own nature, are among the most quoted stanzas of Kashmiri Shaivism.
historicalContext: The Spanda tradition took shape in Kashmir in the ninth century around the work of Vasugupta's line, and Kṣemarāja's commentary made its verses a classical statement of the school beside the Śivasūtra and the Tantrāloka; Sri Aurobindo's later translations brought the text into modern Indian philosophy.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: the fifty-three verses of the whole poem, streamed from GRETIL at read time and indexed in reading order. The file prints no reference abbreviation beside its verses, so the reader follows the number the edition prints at the end of each verse, and the file's own opening heading is not indexed. Because the edition numbers the verses afresh in each of the four sections, a number that occurs again is kept distinct in the index and the reading order decides. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
